newsitem.title: SPAIN: Mass vigil as Spain hunts ETA kidnap victim.
newsitem.headline: Mass vigil as Spain hunts ETA kidnap victim.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Spaniards staged a nationwide silent vigil on Friday while police hunted for a kidnapped politician whom Basque guerrillas have threatened to kill on Saturday.
Crowds gathered outside town and city halls across the country at 1 p.m. (1300 GMT) in support for Miguel Angel Blanco, a local Basque official of the ruling Popular Party kidnapped on Thursday.
The separatist group ETA has threatened to execute Blanco unless the government moves about 500 ETA inmates to Basque country prisons by 4 p.m. on Saturday (1400 GMT).
Short of a last-minute rescue, officials feared they could do little to save Blanco's life after the government ruled out any concessions to what it calls a "band of terrorists".
"We roundly condemn this new act of violence, especially cruel because it makes it impossible for any of us to do something to save this human life," the Basque parliament said in a statement.
In the Basque and Navarre regions, a manhunt was underway with hundreds of police and Civil Guard troops combing the area for the hostage, Interior Ministry sources said.

After the weekly cabinet meeting, the government announced Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar would lead a massive demonstration on Saturday in Bilbao, the Basque industrial centre. It will be only the second time Aznar has visited the troubled Basque region since he took power in May 1996.
Basque leaders urged all citizens to turn out at the Bilbao demonstration which starts at noon (1000 GMT), four hours before the ETA ultimatum expires.
Blanco, 29, was abducted on Thursday shortly after leaving his home in Ermua to catch a train to work. He had just eaten lunch with his parents and was last seen at Ermua train station.
He was probably targeted because he was a member of the ruling party but, as a low-level official, was not protected by bodyguards, authorities said.
Government officials dismissed ETA's demand, saying they would not succumb to blackmail and change the prisoner policy in the face of a threat.
"ETA knows it has set conditions which are impossible to meet," Basque political leaders said in a statement after an emergency meeting.
The Vatican condemned the kidnapping.

"It's an act of terrorism which threatens the life of the hostage, which is an affront to peaceful co-habitation and which offends the sentiments of the noble Spanish people," Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Angelo Sodano wrote.
ETA has been pushing the government to move jailed members to prisons in the Basque region. Many Basque nationalist leaders who oppose ETA have also pressed for a prisoner transfer.
Under a long-standing government policy, the inmates are scattered in small groups around the country.
Spanish newspapers said this was the third time ETA had set a deadline to kill a kidnap victim. In the previous cases, both hostages were killed.
About 800 people have died in ETA's 29-year struggle for an independent Basque homeland.

The latest kidnapping tempered the euphoria that followed the release of two ETA hostages last week. The separatists released kidnapped businessman Cosme Delclaux on July 1 after his family paid the captors $6.85 million.
Hours later, a Civil Guard unit rescued prison worker Jose Antonio Ortega Lara, who had been held for 532 days.

The blue ribbons which symbolise opposition to ETA kidnappings reappeared on newspaper front pages, television screens and public buildings just 10 days after they were taken down in celebration of Delclaux and Ortega Lara's freedom.
